121.quote_or_event: “They conquer the five thieves, and enshrine the True Lord in the heart.”
121.explanation: Guru Nanak teaches that subduing the five thieves (lust, anger, greed, attachment and ego) opens the heart to God.
121.tie_back: The Kural says self-restraint lifts a person to the company of the immortals; in Sikh terms, conquering the five thieves leads to union with God.
121.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 223, Raag Gauree, Guru Nanak (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
121._accuracy_note: Reasonable but partial: restraint of the passions as the way upward is shared, but the verse lacks the Kural's warning of thick darkness, and its goal is God, not the devas.

122.quote_or_event: “Let self-control be the furnace, and patience the goldsmith.”
122.explanation: In the closing pauri of Japji Guru Nanak lists self-control (jat) as the first part of the mint where the true coin of the Shabad is struck.
122.tie_back: The Kural asks us to guard restraint like a treasure; Japji makes self-control the furnace in which life's real gold is made.
122.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 8, Japji Sahib, Pauri 38, Guru Nanak (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
122._accuracy_note: Reasonable fit: self-control as the source of what is most precious; the treasure image is implied rather than stated.

123.quote_or_event: “O Nanak, he is a brave warrior, who conquers and subdues his vicious inner ego.”
123.explanation: Guru Amar Das redefines heroism as the conquest of one's own haumai.
123.tie_back: The Kural says restraint, understood as wisdom, wins recognition from the good; Gurbani gives the person who masters himself the honoured title of true hero.
123.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 86, Siree Raag, Siree Raag ki Vaar, Salok Mahala 3, Guru Amar Das (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
123._accuracy_note: Reasonable fit on self-mastery winning distinction; the Kural's link between restraint and wisdom is not stated.

124.quote_or_event: “Through the Word of the Guru's Shabad, they conquer the five thieves.” … “Even as householders, they lovingly attune themselves to the True Lord.”
124.explanation: Guru Amar Das describes Gurmukhs who master the passions while living the ordinary householder's life.
124.tie_back: Parimelazhagar reads the Kural as praising restraint that never leaves the householder's station; Sikhism likewise sets self-mastery within family life, not in renunciation.
124.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 230, Raag Gauree, Guru Amar Das (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
124._accuracy_note: Strong fit with the householder reading of restraint; the Kural's image of stature higher than a mountain is absent.

125.quote_or_event: “One who has the Guru on his side - how could he be proud of his wealth?”
125.explanation: Bhatt Nal, a court poet whose Savaiye are in the Guru Granth Sahib, says that one guided by the Guru does not grow proud of riches.
125.tie_back: The Kural says humility in the wealthy shines like a second wealth; the Bhatt's verse names that same freedom from the pride wealth breeds.
125.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 1399, Savaiye (Bhatt Nal) (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
125._accuracy_note: Reasonable fit on humility despite riches; it is by a Bhatt rather than a Guru, and it explains humility by the Guru's grace instead of praising it as an adornment.

126.quote_or_event: “I have brought the ten sensory organs under my control, and erased every trace of the five thieves.”
126.explanation: Bhagat Namdev describes bringing all the senses under control and wiping out the passions that ride on them.
126.tie_back: The Kural's tortoise drawing in its limbs is the image of the senses withdrawn and guarded; Namdev's verse states the same mastery of the senses directly.
126.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 693, Raag Dhanaasree, Bhagat Namdev (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
126._accuracy_note: Strong fit on mastery of the senses; there is no tortoise image, and the Kural's protection through seven births is not a Sikh framing.

127.quote_or_event: “and who speaks insipid words with his tongue, is ruined, again and again.”
127.explanation: Guru Amar Das warns that the person whose tongue speaks harsh, insipid words brings ruin on himself over and over.
127.tie_back: The Kural tells us to guard the tongue above all, since those who do not come to grief through their own words; Gurbani says the unguarded tongue leads to repeated ruin.
127.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 594, Raag Vadhans, Guru Amar Das (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
127._accuracy_note: Strong fit on the unguarded tongue bringing self-inflicted ruin; the Kural's 'whatever else you fail to guard' priority is not stated, and the quoted line completes a sentence begun in the previous line.

128.quote_or_event: “Do not utter even a single harsh word; your True Lord and Master abides in all.”
128.explanation: Sheikh Farid, whose saloks are in the Guru Granth Sahib, forbids even one harsh word because the Lord lives in every person addressed.
128.tie_back: The Kural says a single harmful word can turn all one's good to no good; Farid's 'not even a single harsh word' carries the same weight on one utterance.
128.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 1384, Salok Sheikh Farid (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
128._accuracy_note: Strong fit on the gravity of even one harmful word, though Farid gives the reason as God's presence in all rather than the cancelling of one's merit. The same salok was also used (with its following line) for Kural 90.

129.quote_or_event: “Sweetness of honey cannot match the sweetness of sweetly spoken words. No poison is as discomforting as bitter words.”
129.explanation: Bhai Gurdas compares bitter words to poison and sweet words to honey; the next line of the same Kabit sets the coolness of sweet words against the burning heat (tapat) of harsh ones.
129.tie_back: The Kural says the scar of a burning tongue never heals; Bhai Gurdas likewise ranks the injury of harsh words above any physical poison.
129.source: Kabit Savaiye Bhai Gurdas, Kabit 256 (English translation as given in the BaniDB database used by searchgurbani.com)
129._accuracy_note: Reasonable fit on harsh words wounding worse than physical harm; the Kural's contrast of a fire burn that heals and a tongue scar that does not is only implied. Bhai Gurdas's Kabits are early Sikh exegesis, not scripture.

130.quote_or_event: “To practice forgiveness is the true fast, good conduct and contentment.”
130.explanation: Guru Nanak lists forgiveness, good conduct and contentment as the true discipline of the person in whom God dwells.
130.tie_back: The Kural's person who guards against anger and stays restrained is the one Virtue seeks out; Gurbani makes forgiveness (the opposite of anger) and good conduct the real religious practice.
130.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 223, Raag Gauree, Guru Nanak (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
130._accuracy_note: Reasonable fit on curbing anger and practising restraint as the core of virtue; the Kural's personified Virtue waiting for its moment, and its mention of learning, have no counterpart.
